title: Time-Series SQL
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of time-series sql.
Apply grouping events by date in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn time-series sql through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Time-Series SQL matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: In time-series sql, define the unit of analysis before writing the query: one row per customer, order, day, or other grain. Make filters, NULL handling, time boundaries, and tie-breaking rules visible in the SQL.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Grouping events by date, Daily, monthly, and yearly reporting, Rolling time windows, Comparing consecutive periods. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Grouping events by date
items.text: Grouping events by date needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Daily, monthly, and yearly reporting
items.text: Daily, monthly, and yearly reporting begins with a definition of the metric and its grain. Name the numerator, denominator, time zone, null policy, and tie-handling rule before translating the definition into SQL.

items.title: Rolling time windows
items.text: Rolling time windows is easier to reason about when the input row grain, partition keys, ordering, and tie-breaking rule are explicit. A window expression can add a calculation while keeping the individual input rows visible.

items.title: Comparing consecutive periods
items.text: Comparing consecutive periods helps you use SQL for reporting and analysis with the right grain, time buckets, windows, distribution statistics, and business metric definitions. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Time-zone-aware reporting
items.text: Time-zone-aware reporting needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Missing time intervals
items.text: Missing time intervals requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

content_blocks.code: SELECT date_trunc('month', order_date) AS order_month, COUNT(*) AS order_count, SUM(total_amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY date_trunc('month', order_date) ORDER BY order_month;
content_blocks.expected_output: The result groups by calendar month in the timestamp's applicable time zone. For complete time-series reporting, decide whether months with no orders should also appear.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a disposable local PostgreSQL database such as codeleaf_sql_lab after loading datasets/postgresql-lab-setup.sql. Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic grouping events by date and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
